q: Which judicial body was established in Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773, with original and appellate jurisdiction, though its authority often clashed with the council's?
o: The Federal Court
A Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta
The Privy Council
The Sadar Diwani Adalat

q: The Act of 1786 conceded which demand of Lord Cornwallis, subsequently extended to all future governors-general?
o: The power to appoint all district collectors without oversight
The power to unilaterally abolish the Board of Control
The power to declare war without approval from London
The power to override the council's decisions if he assumed personal responsibility for them, and to simultaneously hold the offices of governor-general and commander-in-chief

q: The Charter Act of 1813 set aside one lakh rupees annually for which purpose, an important early statement of state responsibility for education?
o: Revival, promotion and encouragement of literature, learning and science among the natives of India
Compensation to zamindars for lost revenue
Construction of railways across India
Establishment of a national university system

q: Which declaration in the Charter Act of 1833, though poorly implemented in practice, became a foundational plank of Indian political agitation?
o: All revenue collected in India would be spent exclusively within India
Indians would be granted representation in the British Parliament
No Indian citizen was to be denied employment under the Company on grounds of religion, colour, birth or descent
All Indians would automatically receive British citizenship

q: The Act for Better Government of India, 1858, passed in the aftermath of the 1857 revolt, brought about which major change?
o: It transferred all governance to a newly created Indian Parliament
It granted the Congress formal representation in governance
India was to be governed by and in the name of the Crown through a secretary of state (with an advisory council), ending the dual system of Pitt's India Act, and the governor-general became Viceroy
It abolished the office of governor-general entirely

q: The Indian Councils Act, 1892, passed partly in response to Congress demands, introduced which principle, despite carefully avoiding the term 'election'?
o: Direct universal adult suffrage for all legislative council seats
Abolition of the Imperial Legislative Council altogether
An element of indirect election through recommendations by universities, district boards, municipalities, zamindars and chambers of commerce
Reservation of seats exclusively for Congress-nominated candidates

q: What was a significant and problematic feature introduced by the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)?
o: Direct election to the Imperial Legislative Council by popular vote
Complete abolition of all communal representation
Universal adult suffrage for all Indian men regardless of religion
Separate electorates for Muslims, with representation in excess of their population and a lower income qualification for Muslim voters than for Hindus

q: Under the Government of India Act, 1919, the Indian Legislative Council at the Centre was replaced by which bicameral structure?
o: A Rajya Sabha and a Lok Sabha
A Council of State (Upper House) and a Legislative Assembly (Lower House)
A Senate and a House of Representatives
A Federal Assembly and a Provincial Assembly

q: The Simon Commission (Indian Statutory Commission), appointed in November 1927, recommended which of the following in its 1930 report?
o: Abolition of dyarchy, extension of responsible government in the provinces, a federation of British India and princely states, and continuation of communal electorates
Immediate grant of full independence to India with no further review
Permanent retention of dyarchy in both provinces and the Centre
Abolition of all communal electorates with immediate effect

q: Why did the All-India Federation envisaged under the Government of India Act, 1935 never come into existence?
o: Because the princely states unanimously refused to consider the federation from the outset
Because World War II broke out before any implementation could begin
Because the British Parliament formally repealed the federation provisions before implementation
Because of opposition from different Indian parties, leading the British to implement only provincial autonomy (from April 1, 1937) while the Centre continued under the 1919 Act framework

q: How did the maximum permissible age for the ICS entrance examination change over time, as a deliberate barrier to Indian entry?
o: It was gradually raised from 19 to 23 to make the exam more accessible to Indians
It was abolished entirely after the Charter Act of 1853
It remained fixed at 21 throughout the colonial period
It was gradually reduced from 23 (1859) to 22 (1860) to 21 (1866) to 19 (1878, under Lytton)

q: What was the significance of the 1893 House of Commons resolution regarding civil service examinations?
o: It was implemented immediately, resulting in simultaneous exams from 1894 onward
It supported holding simultaneous examinations in India and England but was never actually implemented
It reserved half of all ICS posts for Indians with immediate effect
It abolished the ICS examination altogether

q: The 1902 Police Commission recommended establishing which two bodies for intelligence and criminal investigation?
o: The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in provinces and a Central Intelligence Bureau at the Centre
An All-India Police Force under direct central command
A separate secret police answerable only to the Viceroy
A Federal Investigation Agency modelled on European lines

q: Regarding the British Indian Army's composition before 1857, which of the following is correct?
o: It comprised the 'Queen's army' (Crown troops on duty in India) and separate 'Company's troops' (a mix of European regiments and locally recruited Native regiments under British officers)
It had no European component whatsoever until after 1857
It consisted solely of Indian soldiers with no British troops present at all
It was composed entirely of mercenaries hired from other European colonial powers

q: After 1857, army reorganisation deliberately fixed the ratio of Europeans to Indians in the Bengal Army, and in the Madras and Bombay Armies, at approximately what levels?
o: Complete parity of one European to one Indian everywhere
No fixed ratio was ever established after 1857
One European to two Indians in Bengal, and two Europeans to five Indians in Madras and Bombay
One European to ten Indians in all three armies equally

q: The ideology of 'martial races' and 'non-martial races', developed particularly under Lord Roberts (commander-in-chief, 1887-92), was primarily used to justify:
o: The complete exclusion of all Indians from the army
Equal recruitment opportunities for all Indian communities regardless of region
Discriminatory recruitment favouring groups like Sikhs, Gurkhas and Pathans (who had aided suppression of 1857) over groups from regions that had participated in the revolt
The recruitment of only urban, English-educated Indians into combat roles

q: According to Charles Wood, Secretary of State for India (as quoted in the chapter), what was the underlying purpose of introducing caste and communal companies within Indian army regiments?
o: To reduce costs by grouping soldiers according to dietary preferences
To ensure equal representation of all regions in every regiment for administrative convenience
To cultivate rivalry between different groups (e.g., Sikh versus Hindu, Gorkha versus either) so soldiers would fire on each other without scruple if needed, preventing unified nationalist sentiment
To promote genuine multicultural harmony and unity among Indian soldiers

q: What major judicial reform did Cornwallis introduce regarding the collector's role, marking a key step in the separation of powers?
o: The collector was made responsible only for revenue administration, losing all magisterial functions, which were transferred to a new district judge
The collector was given both revenue and full judicial powers combined for greater efficiency
The collector was made subordinate directly to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat
The office of collector was abolished entirely

q: Which set of codified laws resulted from the Law Commission established under Macaulay in 1833?
o: The Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784)
The Government of India Act (1858) and Indian Councils Act (1861)
The Hindu Code Bill and the Special Marriage Act
The Civil Procedure Code (1859), Indian Penal Code (1860), and Criminal Procedure Code (1861)

q: Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870 is significant in the history of local self-government because it:
o: Abolished all local taxation in favour of central government funding
Established the first fully elected municipal bodies in India
Began the process of financial decentralisation by transferring departments like education, medical services and roads to provincial control, authorising local taxation to fund them
Introduced universal adult franchise for local body elections

q: The Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1908) identified which factor as the greatest obstacle to effective local self-government, and recommended empowering village panchayats with which additional powers?
o: Overcrowded courts; recommended abolishing village panchayats entirely
Lack of financial resources; recommended judicial jurisdiction in petty cases and control over minor village works, schools and fuel/fodder reserves
Excessive local taxation; recommended abolishing all local taxes
Lack of British officials in villages; recommended appointing more European supervisors

q: Under dyarchy (Government of India Act, 1919), why could Indian ministers accomplish little in the sphere of local self-government despite it becoming a 'transferred' subject?
o: Because finance remained a 'reserved' subject under an executive councillor's control, leaving ministers without adequate funds
Because local self-government was entirely removed from provincial jurisdiction
Because the British directly vetoed any local government initiatives
Because the Congress boycotted all provincial ministries during this period

q: The Simon Commission (1930), reviewing local self-government, made which observation regarding elected members and local taxation?
o: It found no issues whatsoever with the state of local self-government
It praised elected members for aggressively and effectively raising local taxes
It noted the reluctance of elected members to impose local taxes and observed a general deterioration in local body finances since the 1919 reforms
It recommended immediate abolition of all local self-governing bodies

q: How did the Government of India Act, 1935 affect local self-governing institutions, notwithstanding the provincial autonomy it introduced?
o: It granted local bodies unrestricted and unprecedented powers of taxation with no restrictions whatsoever
Though provincial autonomy brought portfolio finance under popular ministries (aiding local bodies), new restrictions were also placed on local bodies' power to levy or enhance certain taxes
